subject: Questions on the underlying implementation detail for 'scale' argument.

messages.author: ff1a5632abbf2fe9
messages.subject: Questions on the underlying implementation detail for 'scale' argument.
parts:
Dear INLA experts

Although I have asked a similar question in a previous post, I think it would be better to start a new post on this specific topic.

After reading the help documents on 'scale' argument. I have done some experiment with the data and code in your tutorials 'http://www.r-inla.org/examples/volume-1/code-for-epil-example'. The result is a little weird. There are four ways to implement the formula part, and the 1st one is from the above link.

A: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid") + f(rand,model="iid")
B: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(1,236))
C: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(10000,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))
D: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))

I just report the fixed effect intercept in this post, as the result is lengthy. The other estimated parameters have similar patterns.
                      mean     sd     0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant kld
A: (Intercept)  1.5765 0.0762     1.4242   1.5774     1.7240   0
B: (Intercept)  1.5765 0.0762     1.4242   1.5774     1.7240   0
C: (Intercept)  1.6859 0.0310     1.6245   1.6861     1.7463   0
D: (Intercept)  1.6211 0.0763     1.4684   1.6219     1.7690   0

The inconsistencies between B and C, between B and D, between C and D, made me a little lost. Because my naive thought is that the 'scale' argument is closed in its latent environment f(), just giving the relative weight in that latent environment f(), and there is not interaction between different  f(), or between f() and fixed effect. If that is true, there should be not differences in the four different codes in terms of fixed effect parameter.

Is there something I missed?

Thank you,
Xing

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Questions on the underlying implementation detail for 'scale' argument.
parts:
On 4 September 2013 00:01, Zhao Xing <zhaox...@gmail.com> wrote:
> A: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind, model="iid") +
> f(rand,model="iid")
> B: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind,
> model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(1,236))
> C: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind,
> model="iid",scale=rep(10000,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))
> D: formula = y ~ ClBase4 + CTrt + CBT+ ClAge + CV4 + f(Ind,
> model="iid",scale=rep(1,59)) + f(rand,model="iid",scale=rep(10000,236))

You use the default priors for the f()-precision parameters, and they
are the same for all the cases, but the uniform rescaling of the
entire f()-models is effectively equivalent to rescaling the prior
distributions. I suspect that this explains all the differences in
your results. In essence, one _shouldn't_ get the same results for
case C and D as for A and B.

I think your original purpose for using "scale" was to treat some
effects as "zero effect"? Then this merely shows that you succeeded
(partly; 10000 isn't large enough to actually give zero effects). A
different approach to that would be to set "Ind" and "rand" to NA for
those entries, as that really means "zero effect" when estimating the
model. I think "scale" is more appropriate if you have different, but
finite, known scaling factors for each effect.

> I just report the fixed effect intercept in this post, as the result is
> lengthy. The other estimated parameters have similar patterns.
> mean sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant kld
> A: (Intercept) 1.5765 0.0762 1.4242 1.5774 1.7240 0
> B: (Intercept) 1.5765 0.0762 1.4242 1.5774 1.7240 0
> C: (Intercept) 1.6859 0.0310 1.6245 1.6861 1.7463 0
> D: (Intercept) 1.6211 0.0763 1.4684 1.6219 1.7690 0

> I think "scale" is more appropriate if you have different, but
> finite, known scaling factors for each effect.

Thank you for your thoughtful explanation. So there is a consequent question in terms of the scaling factor.
To make the question concrete, suppose we have two observations, and we have the information that the 'iid' random effect of X1 is twice that of X2. we may set the scale=c(2,1), or scale=c(1,0.5). The other specification like scale=c(100,50) is supposed to rescale the prior as you mentioned.
What do you think?
 
Best,
Xing

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Questions on the underlying implementation detail for 'scale' argument.
parts:
On 4 Sep 2013, at 07:31, ZhaoXing <zhaox...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Finn
 
> I think "scale" is more appropriate if you have different, but
> finite, known scaling factors for each effect.
 
Thank you for your thoughtful explanation. So there is a consequent question in terms of the scaling factor.
To make the question concrete, suppose we have two observations, and we have the information that the 'iid' random effect of X1 is twice that of X2. we may set the scale=c(2,1), or scale=c(1,0.5). The other specification like scale=c(100,50) is supposed to rescale the prior as you mentioned.

Not quite; as written in the documentation at
http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/latent/indep.pdf
the scale applies to the precisions, not the variances, so you need to swap the two numbers.
The way you wrote it above, it would be the _precision_ (=1/variance) of X1 that would be twice as big as for X2.

For each of the three cases, there is a specific set of parameters for the tau-prior that gives equivalent models, so for easier interpretability, keep "scale" close to 1 for "standard" effects, and other values around that for "different" effects.

Finn

What do you think?
 
Best,
Xing
